topic: How Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) Store Facts in Transformers

sections.title: The Analogy: Key-Value Memory
sections.content: Introduce the MLP as a 'knowledge vault.' Explain that while attention mechanisms focus on relationships between words, MLPs act as the internal long-term memory where factual associations are consolidated.
sections.example: Imagine a library where the Attention layer tells you which books to look at, while the MLP is the bookshelf containing the actual facts written on the pages.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Neuron as a Pattern Matcher
sections.content: Briefly define a neuron's activity using the formula y = σ(Wx + b). Visualize this as a light dimmer: if input 'x' matches a specific 'pattern' (weight W), the neuron fires. Higher layers store more abstract concepts.
sections.example: A specific set of neurons 'lighting up' when they see the activation pattern for 'Capital of France' and 'Paris'.

sections.title: Mechanism: Key-Value Memory Pairs
sections.content: Explain that MLPs function as a Key-Value memory. The first layer (expansion) acts as the 'Key' (detecting the context), and the second layer (projection) acts as the 'Value' (inserting the factual output).
sections.example: Input 'Hogwarts' (Key) triggers a neuron that outputs 'Dumbledore' (Value) in the next layer, effectively storing the relation 'Headmaster of Hogwarts = Dumbledore'.

sections.title: Visualizing Weight Updates
sections.content: Show a graphical transition: a single neuron’s weight vector rotating toward a new data point during training. Use an animation of a vector aligning with an 'Fact Vector'.
sections.example: If a model learns 'The Eiffel Tower is in Paris', the weights are mathematically adjusted (gradient descent) to minimize the distance between the model's output and the true fact.

sections.title: Conclusion: Distributed Representation
sections.content: Summarize that facts are not stored in one 'cell', but across a 'distributed' network. Deleting a fact requires re-training, as it is encoded in the precise geometry of high-dimensional weight space.
sections.example: Like a holographic image: if you cut a piece of the film, you don't lose one pixel, but the whole image becomes slightly blurry.
